2699:
Guangxi, 1968

In 1984 a central investigation team counted 89,700 named dead in Guangxi. Of these, 3,700 died in armed fighting and 7,000 were driven to their deaths. The other 79,000 and more were beaten to death or shot in organized killings. The team believed the total was at least 100,000. Most of the dead were from the April 22 faction. Very few were from the Alliance Command. Most of the killings were organized directly by local governments at the county level and below. History See Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 19 (paraphrased).

On July 3, 1968, the Central Committee, the State Council, the Central Military Commission and the Central Cultural Revolution Group jointly issued a proclamation. It addressed the sabotage of railways and the looting of aid supplies bound for Vietnam in Guangxi, and ordered that these be firmly stopped. History

Because of the Nanjing statement, you were called to Beijing to speak about Shanghai's experience at a study class.

The leaders of Guangxi's two factions were staying there too. The April 22 faction had rooms at the east end of the corridor, the Alliance Command at the west end. The canteen served them in two sittings.

On July 3 the Center issued a proclamation. It said that in parts of Guangxi people had sabotaged the railways, looted aid supplies bound for Vietnam and attacked army units, and that this must be firmly stopped. The proclamation was read out at the study class. When it was over, the April 22 people said nothing at all.

That night one of the April 22 leaders knocked on your door. He was about thirty, a worker at a machinery plant in Nanning. He said, you have two factions in Shanghai too, how did you get them to sit down together. Then he asked one more thing. What will happen to us when we go back.

You knew the proclamation had already gone out. You also knew nothing you said would change what happened in Guangxi.

2721:
Technicians in the Factory

In 1971 and 1972 the national average pass rate for industrial products was only about 45%. In Tianjin, factories did about four hours of real work in an eight-hour shift. At one dye plant, a batch was held at temperature one hour too short and the whole batch was scrapped. Technicians earned less than workers who had started in the same year. A technician who graduated from a technical school in 1957 made 48.50 yuan in 1972. An apprentice who started that same year had become a grade-four worker by 1972 and made 57.60 yuan. History See Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 30 (paraphrased).

Joel Andreas writes about the experience of Tsinghua's university-run factory. Early in the Cultural Revolution the workers elected their own interim leadership, but a general meeting spent a whole day on working hours and could not decide. One manager said, how do you lead a hundred people. The people most easily hurt by workers' self-management were the factory's intellectuals. Interpretation See Rise of the Red Engineers (《红色工程师的崛起》), ch. 6 (paraphrased).

He made 52 yuan a month, a few yuan less than a maintenance fitter in the shop who had started the same year. The report ran 11 pages. It said nobody controlled temperature and humidity to the process standard, machine speeds were set by whoever ran them, and top rollers were not replaced when they should have been. The last sentence read, I propose that the original process rules be restored and strictly enforced.

At the meeting, a workers' representative elected by the shop read the report aloud. When he reached the last sentence, someone laughed. A loom tender said, the original rules are the ones that docked our pay. Another said, how many times a year does a technician even come down to the shop.

Yan Zhicheng sat in a corner and said nothing. He held a pencil in his hand the whole time.

The chairman of the factory revolutionary committee phoned the city and asked you what to do.

2734:
Worker-Cadres

In the 1970s, a worker promoted to a cadre post could keep worker status and the original wage grade. This was called being a “worker-cadre”. After 1980, cadres were generally no longer promoted directly from among workers. The worker-cadre system was abolished, and there were no more calls for cadres to do manual labor or for workers to take part in management. History See Joel Andreas, Rise of the Red Engineers (《红色工程师的崛起》), ch. 10 (paraphrased).

She said she did not want to switch. But if she did not, the mill said, then you are a worker, and a worker running a workshop has no proper title.

Worker-cadre was the term in those years. A worker who was promoted kept worker status and the original wage grade, and still went back to work in the shop. Some people switched to cadre status as soon as they were promoted and never went back to the shop again.

2746:
Recommendation and Exams

Recommendation of worker-peasant-soldier students had three steps. The masses recommended, the leadership approved, and the university reviewed. How democratic it was depended on the leaders of the work unit. Tsinghua teachers sent out to recruit would visit coworkers, and once turned down the son of a prefecture cadre. Workers said, in the factory we have power, but higher up we have none. In Tsinghua's first class of worker-peasant-soldier students in 1970, the share from worker and poor and lower-middle peasant families rose from under 37% before the Cultural Revolution to 81%. But cadres' children were concentrated in the good majors. History See Joel Andreas, Rise of the Red Engineers (《红色工程师的崛起》), ch. 8 (paraphrased).

In April 1973 academic testing was restored. The top scores mostly went to urban sent-down youth. The universities wanted to admit by score. Local officials wanted to admit rural youth who had returned home. Zhang Tiesheng handed in a blank exam paper, and the testing was dropped. That autumn and winter, Chi Qun and others gave 613 professors a surprise exam. Two hundred of them handed in blank papers. History Ibid., same chapter (paraphrased).

Andreas concludes that the recommendation system broke the passing of cultural capital from one generation to the next, but could become a way of reproducing political capital. Interpretation

Rebels in Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius

Rebels across the country treated the Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius campaign of early 1974 as a chance to come back. People who had been persecuted got their files back, and some burned the materials used against them on the spot. In Shanghai, by 1972, nearly half of the mass representatives in the leadership of industrial, financial and trade units had already been purged.
